{"id": "2:31/q38", "question": "How do inflected and fixed Arabic endings differ?", "turns_on": "Sībawayh separates changing case or mood endings from built forms.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q38/p1", "position": "Nouns and imperfect verbs have changing case or mood endings; built forms retain fixed endings.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives eight paired pronunciations and details noun cases, imperfect moods, past and imperative forms, dual and plural markers, diptotes, gender, number and definiteness. Qur'an 16:124 exemplifies an imperfect with lām; adjective and broken-plural patterns govern diptote behavior."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q39", "question": "What is knowledge, as invoked by Adam's lesson?", "turns_on": "Theological, Muʿtazilite and philosophical definitions differ; al-Rāzī argues for its self-evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q39/p1", "position": "Knowledge is what makes a knower know, or true apprehension or disclosure of the known.", "reasons": "Al-Ashʿarī, al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr, al-Isfarāyīnī, Ibn Fūrak and al-Qaffāl offer formulations. Al-Rāzī tests each for circularity, exclusion of divine or non-action knowledge, and obscurity."}, {"id": "2:31/q39/p2", "position": "Knowledge is certain belief producing tranquility of soul.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazila give this account; Rāzī's associates object that belief is distinct from knowledge and divine knowledge has no soul's tranquility. The Muʿtazila answer with a common element of belief."}, {"id": "2:31/q39/p3", "position": "Knowledge is a form or image in the soul corresponding to the object.", "reasons": "Philosophers and al-Ghazālī compare cognition to a mirror image. Rāzī objects from absent objects, abstract relations, nonexistents, perception's location, heat and the philosophers' own account of mirrors."}, {"id": "2:31/q39/p4", "position": "Knowledge is too immediately evident to define by something clearer.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues everyone directly knows their existence and place; knowing a relation requires knowing its terms. Failed definitions may reflect this extreme obviousness."}, {"id": "2:31/q39/p5", "position": "Belief varies from certain true understanding to false certainty, doubt, expectation and illusion.", "reasons": "Al-Juwaynī divides immediate, inferred and imitative certainty and uncertain belief; al-Rāzī says flaws remain to be discussed."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q40", "question": "How do Arabic terms for knowing differ?", "turns_on": "Different terms describe perception, memory, reasoning, conjecture, skill and wisdom.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q40/p1", "position": "Terms such as perception, awareness, conception, preservation, remembrance and understanding describe stages or modes of knowing.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī distinguishes idrāk, shuʿūr, taṣawwur, ḥifẓ, tadhakkur and dhikr, raising a paradox about commanded remembrance and answering from introspective capacity. He further defines fahm, fiqh, ʿaql, dirāya and ḥikma, distinguishing divine from human usage."}, {"id": "2:31/q40/p2", "position": "Knowledge may be certain, conjectural, intuitive, experienced or inferred by signs.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī surveys yaqīn, thought, intuition, quick intelligence, first principles, deliberation, practical discernment, experience, opinion and physiognomy; he distinguishes praiseworthy evidence-based conjecture from blameworthy weak conjecture and sensory image from sleeping apparition."}, {"id": "2:31/q40/p3", "position": "Maʿrifa is particular knowledge, conceptual grasp, or recognition after earlier perception.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports three analyses and says grasp of God's essence is beyond people; one may assent to the Necessary Being without such maʿrifa."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q41", "question": "What examples are given of knowledge's practical power?", "turns_on": "The sources offer legal, rhetorical and advisory cases rather than a single event.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q41/p1", "position": "Legal learning and verbal ingenuity resolve difficult disputes or avert danger.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī recounts Abū Yūsuf on theft and oaths, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar on maternal descent, Abū Ḥanīfa on representation, vows, theft and marriage, al-Shāfiʿī on consensus, and poets and courtiers escaping punishment through wording. His reports also mention ingenious answers about a ruler's fear and learning."}, {"id": "2:31/q41/p2", "position": "Knowledge and action improve souls, while ignorance and love of the world obstruct them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares learning with life, repentance and light, cites the ant's knowledgeable leadership and a trained dog's purified catch, and says the heart rules by knowledge. His verse and reports urge study, reflection, defense of truth and righteous practice."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q42", "question": "What reports about Adam's creation and the surrounding events are cited?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in details of earth gathering, body formation and sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q42/p1", "position": "God formed Adam from mixed earth, producing human variety.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī and the Prophet describe varied earth and the Angel of Death's handful; al-Qurṭubī says al-Tirmidhī grades the Prophetic report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Bursevī adds Earth refusing Gabriel, Michael and Isrāfīl, weeping springs, forty cubits and return of bodies to their soil."}, {"id": "2:31/q42/p2", "position": "Adam's clay body was formed, lay for a period, then received the spirit; Iblis refused prostration.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's account gives sticky clay, forty years, Iblis testing the hollow body, Adam sneezing and praising God, haste for fruit, and all angels but Iblis prostrating. Biqāʿī debates whether creation and prostration precede the naming demonstration."}, {"id": "2:31/q42/p3", "position": "A report places soil through Adam across Saturday to Friday, but its attribution and chronology are disputed.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī quotes Abū Hurayra's schedule; al-Mizzī notes a view that it came from Kaʿb. Al-Ṭabarī resolves a tension by saying days were named before their spans and Saturday's soil preceded Saturday's created reality."}, {"id": "2:31/q42/p4", "position": "Some angels who questioned Adam repented, and some reports add punishment or the Hārūt and Mārūt trial.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī records Ibn ʿAbbās's troops-of-Iblis narrative, private angelic boasting, a burning-fire report, and the story in which Hārūt and Mārūt's censure of humans led to testing with desire and wine."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q43", "question": "What parallel account of Adam and naming is reported from the Torah?", "turns_on": "The Torah narrative differs in chronology and episodes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q43/p1", "position": "The quoted Torah has Adam naming living creatures after their creation and before the woman is made from his rib.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī recounts heaven and earth, vegetation, lights, animals and humanity, then Eden, rivers and the forbidden tree; the serpent's deception, expulsion, cherub and Adam's 930 years follow. He explains cherub and compares textual versions."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q44", "question": "May earlier scriptures be consulted or transmitted while discussing Adam?", "turns_on": "Permissibility varies with alteration, reader expertise and ritual state.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q44/p1", "position": "Qualified scholars may consult and transmit useful earlier-scripture material, without affirming unverified claims.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī cites 3:93, 5:48, the Prophet's Torah use in an adultery case, permission to narrate Israelite reports and counsel neither to affirm nor deny them. Ibn Ḥajar limits consultation to grounded scholars; al-Shāfiʿī allows useful books after inspection."}, {"id": "2:31/q44/p2", "position": "Torah and Gospel use is restricted because of alteration, with some rulings depending on ritual impurity.", "reasons": "Al-Rāfiʿī and others forbid use of altered books; Biqāʿī limits this to known alteration. Al-Nawawī reports a preferred rule for touching during minor impurity, al-Baghawī allows some utterance during major impurity, and al-Qāḍī al-Ḥusayn gives a disputed extreme ruling."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q45", "question": "How is divine revelation said to be delivered?", "turns_on": "Direct hearing versus transmission of meaning or exact wording.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q45/p1", "position": "Gabriel hears God's revelation and conveys it, while reported accounts distinguish relaying meaning from exact dictation.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī cites heavenly trembling and chain-like sound reports and favors hearing; Abū Shāma connects descent language to Sunni eternal-Qur'an doctrine. Al-Juwaynī distinguishes equivalent expression from fixed dictated words."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q46", "question": "What other general observations about names are adduced?", "turns_on": "Miscellaneous naming and plural observations.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q46/p1", "position": "Names may be shared or multiplied, and spelling, plurality and derivation depend on usage.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī notes shared or multiple sura names and prophetic names; al-Burhān discusses alif deletion in common foreign names and paucity plural patterns. These illustrate broader naming conventions."}]}

{"id": "2:31/q49", "question": "What does the challenge imply about God's authority to choose Adam?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q49/p1", "position": "God's command and choice rest on His knowledge and sovereignty, not on creatures' judgment of what seems preferable.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says God may command whom He wills and that good or bad follows divine judgment; Bursevī contrasts angelic worship with divine grace."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q50", "question": "How are the angels' response and their limited knowledge described?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q50/p1", "position": "They admitted inability and learned that knowledge is God's gift.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī report the admission; al-Ḥaralī treats it as submission and recognition that none has independent knowledge."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q51", "question": "What does ‘upon the angels’ modify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q51/p1", "position": "The prepositional phrase attaches to ‘displayed them.’", "reasons": "Al-Samīn explicitly gives this syntactic attachment."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q52", "question": "What other name is reported for Adam?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q52/p1", "position": "Adam reportedly named himself Īsh, though Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests the reported form may be a corruption of Īth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports that the Arabic Encyclopedia glosses Īsh as 'possessor of acquisition' and translates it as human or reader; he suspects the form was Īth and points to his discussion of 2:35."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q53", "question": "How is the hamza in al-asmāʾ treated in recitation?", "turns_on": "Reader-specific treatment of the hamza.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q53/p1", "position": "Ḥamza pauses before the hamza in al-asmāʾ and similar words.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports Ḥamza's pause before the hamza in al-arḍ, al-asmāʾ and al-ākhira, while other readers do not pause."}, {"id": "2:31/q53/p2", "position": "Warsh transfers the hamza's vowel to the preceding consonant and omits the hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports this rule for Warsh from Nāfiʿ both within words and across word boundaries, citing 23:1 and 28:71."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q54", "question": "What gender is used in commands addressed to the angels?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q54/p1", "position": "Commands to the angels throughout the Qur'an use the masculine form.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī cites usjudū, anbiʾūnī and faqaʿū lahu sājidīn as examples."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q01", "question": "Who says “They said,” and to what challenge do they reply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q01/p1", "position": "The speakers are the angels, answering God's challenge to name what Adam learned.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Jishumī identify the angels. Muqātil says God confronted their claim to knowledge of unseen, uncreated things by asking about visible things they did not know. Ibn Masʿūd's report relates the challenge to their earlier prediction of human corruption. Al-Ālūsī and Bursawī read this as a fresh answer to whether they fulfilled the task."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q02", "question": "Why does “they said” lack a linking particle?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q02/p1", "position": "Direct, successive dialogue needs no conjunction when its sequence is clear.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān cites the dialogue in 2:30, 2:32, 5:27, 2:259, 2:260 and 26:10; al-Ālūsī notes frequent Qurʾānic usage, especially al-Shuʿarāʾ. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifically explains the absence of fa as direct dialogue."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q03", "question": "What does “Subḥānaka” mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is explained by disavowal and transcendence or a movement metaphor.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q03/p1", "position": "It glorifies God by declaring Him transcendent, free of evil, defect, or blame.", "reasons": "Majāz cites al-Aʿshā's poetic repudiation of ʿAlqama's boast; Akhfash uses the same line for disavowal. Ibn ʿAbbās says free of evil; ʿAlī calls it a word God loves; Maymūn calls it a divine name of magnification; al-Ḥasan says humans cannot claim it. Al-Zajjāj reports philologists' agreement on freedom from defect. Abū Ḥayyān contrasts taqdīs as purification, supported by Bayt al-Maqdis, holy land, quds vessel and qidās string of pearls; he also records al-Zamakhsharī's travel derivation and an anonymous poetic qidās."}, {"id": "2:32/q03/p2", "position": "It denotes rapid movement toward God.", "reasons": "Al-Naḍr transmits a dream interpreter's gloss, relating it to a horse's swift swimming motion."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q04", "question": "What is the form and derivation of subḥān?", "turns_on": "Its morphological source, lexicalized status, and the evidence of rare poetic forms.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q04/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun or noun standing for tasbīḥ, normally accusative in an understood glorification construction.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Ṭabarī, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and others give an implicit verb; Sībawayh distinguishes the verbal noun tasbīḥ from its substitute subḥān. Bayḍāwī compares ghufrān and maʿādh Allāh and notes an exceptional predicate use. Ibn ʿĀshūr considers a lighter sabbaḥa derivation; al-Itqān says the verb fell out of use. Samīn records both verbal noun and ism maṣdar analyses."}, {"id": "2:32/q04/p2", "position": "It is a conventional proper name for glorification or transcendence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn discuss standalone poetic subḥān: tanwīn may be poetic declension or indefiniteness, and the untanwinned form diptote through properness plus alif-nūn. Al-Ālūsī cites the al-ʿAlqama poem for naming and the counterclaim of omitted Allāh; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites al-Nābigha's analogous names, while Sībawayh explains loss of tanwīn by definiteness. Bursawī and Elmalılı also call it a proper name."}, {"id": "2:32/q04/p3", "position": "An unusual derivation links it to raising the voice in praise.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaṣṣal derives it from sabaḥa and cites a poem of Taghlib and pilgrims praising God."}, {"id": "2:32/q04/p4", "position": "It is a reduplicated form denoting repeated sanctification.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because it requires unattested singular subḥā; al-Ālūsī objects to the required dual or nominative form and unexplained fixed nūn."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q05", "question": "How is “Subḥānaka” governed and what does its suffix mark?", "turns_on": "Whether it is an accusative cognate noun, vocative, or governed by the quotation verb; whether its suffix denotes object or subject.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q05/p1", "position": "It is accusative with an implied glorification verb, and the kāf is its object.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh supply 'we glorify You'; Abū Ḥayyān says the cognate verb must be omitted and favors object kāf. Samīn also reports annexation to the object."}, {"id": "2:32/q05/p2", "position": "It is an annexed vocative, ‘O Your Glory.’", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī proposes the vocative; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it for lacking a transmitted vocative particle, Samīn says most grammarians reject it, and al-Ālūsī finds no proof."}, {"id": "2:32/q05/p3", "position": "Its accusative is governed by the verb ‘they said.’", "reasons": "Samīn explicitly names the verb of saying as the governing ʿāmil."}, {"id": "2:32/q05/p4", "position": "The kāf can be the subject of the annexation: ‘You are transcendent.’", "reasons": "Samīn reports the subject annexation; Abū Ḥayyān allows that some take the suffix as subject, while favoring object."}, {"id": "2:32/q05/p5", "position": "Al-Kisāʾī explains its accusative by its lack of an adjective.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās transmits this additional grammatical explanation alongside al-Kisāʾī's vocative allowance; Thaʿlabī says it lies outside ordinary description."}, {"id": "2:32/q05/p6", "position": "Standalone subḥān is cut from annexation and therefore takes tanwīn.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says grammar works reject this account; an alternative likens the untanwinned standalone form to qabl and baʿd."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q06", "question": "What are the angels doing by opening with “Subḥānaka”?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is primarily disavowal, apology for the prior question, or courtly praise.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q06/p1", "position": "They clear God of objection, error, or lack of wisdom and disclaim their own claim.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAbbās relate it to God alone knowing the unseen; Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān relate it to His judgment and governance. Abū ʿAlī stresses reverent speech even before knowing the wisdom. Bursawī says God is free of purposeless acts."}, {"id": "2:32/q06/p2", "position": "They apologize or repent for their earlier question or presumption.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr describe apology and courtesy, comparing Moses' 7:143 and Jonah's 21:87; Bursawī notes the same formulas. Those who think angels sinned see repentance; al-Ālūsī says it resembles repentance for a less preferable act without breaching infallibility. Qatāda and al-Ḥasan report the angels had privately claimed superiority."}, {"id": "2:32/q06/p3", "position": "They begin with reverent praise before acknowledging inability.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says praise precedes excuse; Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes majesty. Wāḥidī refers back to the angels' tasbīḥ in 2:30."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q07", "question": "What do the angels mean by “We have no knowledge except what You taught us”?", "turns_on": "Their prior question in 2:30, whether it was culpable, and what God had previously taught them.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q07/p1", "position": "Their knowledge is received from God, and the requested names were not among what He taught them.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, Ibn Isḥāq and many others read it as admi

tting the limit of angelic knowledge. Jishumī and Ṭabrisī specify the names; al-Ālūsī adds inability for the succession task. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the statement admits incapacity rather than informing God. Study Quran stresses limited comprehensive scope."}, {"id": "2:32/q07/p2", "position": "They ask tactfully to be taught and repent for their uninformed question about Adam.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī reports that their ignorance of names reveals greater ignorance of unseen outcomes and warns against rating their own obedience; the reading ties back to 2:30."}, {"id": "2:32/q07/p3", "position": "They express astonishment at being asked about something unknown.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports this further reading."}, {"id": "2:32/q07/p4", "position": "They repent because their earlier speech was a sin.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit this from those who deny angelic infallibility; al-Ālūsī reports and qualifies it."}, {"id": "2:32/q07/p5", "position": "They make an innocent inquiry: God had told them of future corruption but not the names.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān distinguish the earlier divinely supplied prediction from the names; Bayḍāwī, Bursawī and Elmalılı deny an explicit claim to succession or sinful objection."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q08", "question": "How does the wording “no knowledge except what You taught us” add to a bare admission of ignorance?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception acknowledges knowledge already granted or is read hypothetically of future teaching.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q08/p1", "position": "The exception praises God, thanks Him for teaching, and denies independent knowledge.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says 'we do not know this' would omit recognition; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī say a bare denial would miss gratitude and duty. Al-Ālūsī says the broad wording avoids self-assertion and a narrow denial of names. Abū Ḥayyān points to lā with an indefinite noun excluding every kind of untaught knowledge."}, {"id": "2:32/q08/p2", "position": "The wording allows future learning without affirming past teaching.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān sketches a strained disconnected exception with conditional mā: 'whatever You teach us, we shall know'; he says it conflicts with reports of prior divine teaching or knowledge from the Preserved Tablet, unless the angels discount that specific information."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q09", "question": "How is “lā ʿilma lanā” constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether lā is the genus-negating particle or operates like laysa.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q09/p1", "position": "Lā negates an indefinite noun generally; lanā is its omitted locative predicate.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās compares lā rayba fīhi; Ṭabrisī supplies an omitted element governing lanā. Abū Ḥayyān says the indefinite denies every category of knowledge."}, {"id": "2:32/q09/p2", "position": "Lā can instead function as laysa.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās gives the alternative analysis of 'we have no knowledge.'"}]}
{"id": "2:32/q10", "question": "What does ʿilm mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q10/p1", "position": "It can mean the thing known, so the sentence says they know no object except what God taught.", "reasons": "Nasafī explicitly glosses ʿilm as maʿlūm; Samīn uses that sense to explain an omitted resumptive pronoun in the relative clause."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q11", "question": "What is the grammatical role and sense of “mā” after “except”?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is relative, verbal-noun, or conditional; whether the exception is connected, and what can govern mā.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q11/p1", "position": "It is relative, ‘that which You taught us,’ most plausibly nominative in apposition.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers nominative relative mā; Samīn compares lā rayba fīhi and supplies an omitted resumptive if ʿilm means maʿlūm. Naḥḥās compares lā ilāha illā Allāh; al-Ālūsī reports the majority's relative analysis, allowing apposition or accusative exception. Al-Burhān notes relative mā after illā."}, {"id": "2:32/q11/p2", "position": "It is a verbal noun, ‘Your teaching of us,’ taking exception case or nominative apposition.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī gives the verbal-noun sense. Samīn allows accusative as exception and denies government by the noun of lā, which would then have to decline. Bursawī makes the phrase nominative as a substitute for the position of lā ʿilm; Naḥḥās permits accusative after a complete clause."}, {"id": "2:32/q11/p3", "position": "It is nominative as a substitute for lā's predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya analogizes lā ilāha illā Allāh; Samīn objects that exception comes from the judged subject rather than its predicate."}, {"id": "2:32/q11/p4", "position": "It is the accusative object of the following ʿallamtanā.", "reasons": "Al-Zahrawī's proposal is transmitted by Ibn ʿAṭiyya; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn object that a relative clause cannot govern its antecedent. Al-Ālūsī also transmits a remote disconnected-exception rescue."}, {"id": "2:32/q11/p5", "position": "It can be conditional in a disconnected exception, with an omitted answer.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān offers this as strained, and Samīn reports the shaykh's rescue; al-Ālūsī repeats it. It gives 'but whatever You taught us, we knew' or future learning, with no prior knowledge affirmed."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q12", "question": "What does God's teaching imply about the source of knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether establishing evidence counts as God's teaching or teaching requires His production of the resulting knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q12/p1", "position": "God produces acquired knowledge in creatures.", "reasons": "Rāzī presents the Ashʿarite inference and argues evidence alone is not teaching since the learner's own consideration would produce knowledge. He says God alone can produce knowledge in another and cites 55:2. Ṭabrisī also says all knowledge traces to God, though by necessary creation and proof for inference."}, {"id": "2:32/q12/p2", "position": "God teaches by instruction or by establishing evidence from which a learner reasons.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the Muʿtazilite account but rejects evidence alone as sufficient teaching. Ṭabrisī describes necessary knowledge produced by God and inferential knowledge based on proofs He establishes. An astrologer could answer that planetary motions are divine signs, showing the breadth of this account."}]}

{"id": "2:32/q18", "question": "How is “anta” parsed and what does it convey?", "turns_on": "Whether anta is a separator, accusative emphasis, or an independent nominative subject.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q18/p1", "position": "It is a separating pronoun, emphasizing and restricting the divine predicates.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās reports the Kūfan ʿimād; Ṭabrisī, Nasafī, Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr allow faṣl. {"id": "2:32/q19", "question": "How does “al-Ḥakīm” relate syntactically to “al-ʿAlīm”?", "turns_on": "Whether the second divine name is attributive or predicative.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q19/p1", "position": "It is an adjective modifying al-ʿAlīm.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās states the modifying analysis; Samīn lists it as an option and says both forms carry intensive force."}, {"id": "2:32/q19/p2", "position": "It is a second predicate.", "reasons": "Samīn and Nasafī allow the two names as predicates after anta or after inna if anta is a separator."}]}
{"id": "2:32/q20", "question": "Why does “al-ʿAlīm” precede “al-Ḥakīm”?", "turns_on": "Whether the order follows conceptual dependence, the immediate verbal context, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q20/p1", "position": "Knowledge is prior because wisdom depends on it.", "reasons": "Samīn, al-Burhān and al-Ālūsī say sound judgment follows knowledge; al-Burhān adds that knowledge may lead as an essential attribute."}, {"id": "2:32/q20/p2", "position": "It echoes the preceding talk of knowledge and God's command to inform Him.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān points to 'we have no knowledge'; Samīn and al-Ālūsī cite the same local context, al-Ālūsī also the preceding 'inform Me.'"}]}

{"id": "2:32/q22", "question": "What is the force of “Indeed You are the All-Knowing, the Wise” in this reply?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing titles express a general divine perfection or point specifically to Adam's appointment.", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q22/p1", "position": "It confirms their limited knowledge by affirming God's comprehensive knowledge and wise decision.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says Adam's learning shows wisdom in the vicegerency; al-Ālūsī says the clause confirms their denial and corrects a possible misunderstanding. {"id": "2:32/q23", "question": "What conduct does the angels' admission teach a person asked about what they do not know?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q23/p1", "position": "Admit ignorance humbly, say ‘I do not know’ or ‘God knows best,’ and accept correction.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī cites a prophetic warning that ignorant opinion misleads, the Prophet's consultation with Gabriel and Michael on places, Abū Bakr on inheritance, ʿAlī and Ibn ʿUmar on 'God knows best,' Qāsim and Mālik's practice, and the poem of Yazīd. {"id": "2:32/q24", "question": "Does the command to name the things prove God may impose an impossible task?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:32/q24/p1", "position": "Yes: God asked the angels to report names He knew they could not know.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī explicitly draws this inference; Qushayrī says no one can blame God for testing the unable. {"id": "2:40/q08", "question": "What does 'remember' ask them to do?", "turns_on": "Whether recollection alone or gratitude is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q08/p1", "position": "Preserve the favor in heart and memory, without forgetting.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya oppose recollection to forgetting; Qurtubi regards inward retention as a good explanation."}, {"id": "2:40/q08/p2", "position": "Give thanks, praise and obey the Giver.", "reasons": "Baghawi transmits Hasan; Kashshaf requires recognition, magnification and obedience; Ibn Jawzi says memory without gratitude is incomplete; Wahidi identifies belief in Muhammad as required gratitude."}, {"id": "2:40/q08/p3", "position": "Bring something to attention by heart or tongue.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisi list honor, scripture, prayer and speech among dhikr's uses; Harali defines recalling what was forgotten."}]}

{"id": "2:40/q10", "question": "What does niʿmah mean?", "turns_on": "Whether a benefit's ultimate outcome affects its name.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q10/p1", "position": "A bestowed benefit intended kindly.", "reasons": "Damghani and Ibn Jawzi gloss favor; Jishumi requires good intent; Razi excludes pure harm, self-serving help and poisoned gifts; Harali includes bodily and spiritual suitability."}, {"id": "2:40/q10/p2", "position": "All benefits ultimately come from God.", "reasons": "Razi cites 16:53 and 31:14: God creates intermediaries, capacity, motive and guidance; people may still be thanked, as a hadith says."}, {"id": "2:40/q10/p3", "position": "Worldly benefits bless even disbelievers.", "reasons": "Razi prefers Baqillani, citing creation, provision, rescue, security and prosperity; the dispute is partly terminological."}, {"id": "2:40/q10/p4", "position": "Worldly benefits that end in eternal harm are not blessings to disbelievers.", "reasons": "Some Sunnis compare them to poisoned sweets and cite 3:178."}, {"id": "2:40/q10/p5", "position": "All accountable people receive equal religious aid; some also require the best worldly aid.", "reasons": "Razi attributes the latter to Baghdadi Mu'tazilites, not Basrans; Sunnis say God creates both benefits and harms."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q11", "question": "Which favor or favors are recalled?", "turns_on": "Whether examples restrict the unspecified favor.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q11/p1", "position": "Israel's many historic favors, including favors to ancestors.", "reasons": "Sources enumerate rescue from Pharaoh, the parted sea, land, prophets, books, manna, quails, shade, springs, pardon and Torah. Ibn Abbas adds nighttime light, unworn clothes and untangled hair; 5:20 is a parallel."}, {"id": "2:40/q11/p2", "position": "The Torah's knowledge of Muhammad and life in his era.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari says failing to follow him is like forgetting entrusted knowledge; Kashshaf and Nasafi count reaching his time as favor; Elmali emphasizes guidance."}, {"id": "2:40/q11/p3", "position": "All favors, beginning with creation, faculties and Islam.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls Islam greatest (49:17); Jishumi and Tabrisi include reason, senses, provision and protection; Ibn Atiyya prefers the generic word over restricted examples."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q12", "question": "Why can singular niʿmah mean many favors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q12/p1", "position": "It is a generic or collective singular.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Tabrisi and others cite 14:34 or 16:18; Ibn Jawzi compares Arabic singulars used collectively."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q13", "question": "How do favors to ancestors count for descendants?", "turns_on": "Ancestral benefit and the motive for direct address.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q13/p1", "position": "Descendants inherit ancestral benefit and honor.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites Arabic attribution of forebears' deeds to descendants; Razi adds existence itself; Alusi invokes shared religious inheritance."}, {"id": "2:40/q13/p2", "position": "Naming their own favor encourages gratitude over envy.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi note that people readily value their own gifts; attribution to God directs gratitude to Him."}, {"id": "2:40/q13/p3", "position": "Recalling past gifts raises hope for future favor.", "reasons": "Razi says a repeated benefactor is expected to continue kindness, restraining opposition."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q14", "question": "How is the yāʾ of niʿmatī read?", "turns_on": "Resolution of yāʾ before connecting alif.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q14/p1", "position": "Vowel it with fatḥa before the article.", "reasons": "Farra, Akhfash, Zajjaj, Tabrisi and Ibn Atiyya prefer preserving the letter and avoiding two silent letters; Abu Hayyan and Alusi say the seven readers agree."}, {"id": "2:40/q14/p2", "position": "Leave it still, dropping it where two sukūns meet.", "reasons": "Farra permits this before alif-lam and discusses hamza contexts and 39:53/17; Baydawi notes a pause/connection practice."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q15", "question": "How is the yāʾ of biʿahdī read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q15/p1", "position": "It remains quiescent before the following alif.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid records unmoved forms, Nafi's general vocalization rule and exceptions, Ibn Jammaz and Ismail ibn Ja'far's still yāʾ; Nashr says readers agree here because of the many letters. Al-Farisi reports Ahmad ibn Jammaz and Ismail ibn Ja'far transmitting Nafi's still ya' in further forms before a cut hamza and a non-jussive verb."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q16", "question": "How is the relative phrase constructed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q16/p1", "position": "Allatī modifies niʿmah; the relative clause omits a resumptive object.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi supply 'I bestowed it'; Samin cites a 9:69 reading for deletion after preposition loss."}, {"id": "2:40/q16/p2", "position": "The clause clarifies and widens the favor.", "reasons": "Harali interprets allatī as initially vague; Samin says ʿalaykum conveys comprehensive reach."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q17", "question": "What does ʿahd mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q17/p1", "position": "A pledge, testament or undertaking to preserve and fulfill.", "reasons": "Mawardi cites scripture and oath; Jishumi says command/testament; Tabatabai derives preservation; Biqai's Harali, Isfahani and Khalil describe prior private undertaking and continual tending; Kur'an Yolu lists compact, promise and oath."}, {"id": "2:40/q17/p2", "position": "It can name the Mosaic law and the many divine duties.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur notes Israel's scripture uses covenant for law; Kur'an Yolu relates Old and New Testaments to covenant obligations."}]}
